title: Ponding Water on a Low-Slope Roof
description: Water still sitting two days after a Houston rain is ponding. The drains can be open and the middle of a low-slope roof can still hold a pond.
html:
A flat roof is not flat, or it should not be. It is a low slope aimed at drains or scuppers. When water is still standing in the middle two days after the rain stopped, and the drains are open, the roof is holding a pond. That pond cooks in the sun, weighs on the deck, and ages the membrane faster than the field that dried in an hour.

A clear drain can still leave a pond

Clogged drains are the first thing to check, and they are maintenance, not a mystery. Leaves, a plastic bag, a failed strainer. Clear them and a lot of “ponding” leaves with the next rain. If the drains run and the water remains, the deck has deflected or the insulation was never tapered. The low spot is structural or it was built in. More sealant in the middle of the pond does not give the water a direction.

The practical test we use: after a dry stretch, if water is still there forty-eight hours later, call it ponding. A shallow sheet that dries the same day is a low slope doing what low slopes do. Do not let a photo of a wet roof, taken during the storm, become a replacement proposal. Do not ignore a pond you can see on Wednesday from a Monday rain.

What actually moves the water

Crickets and tapered insulation send water to the drain. A new membrane over the same low spot reproduces the pond. Where the structure has sagged, the framing conversation comes before the roofing one. We can patch a leak at the pond. We will not pretend a patch teaches water to run uphill.

Drain sizing and overflow are their own subject, covered in commercial roof drainage. Ponding is what is left when the drains already work. If that is your building, start with a condition report. Call (281) 541-0027 or request the inspection.
